title: Product sense
summary: Learn to judge what makes a product good, and to design a better one for a clear user.

lessons.title: What makes a product good
teach: A good product solves a real problem for a clear user, simply, and better than what they used before.
Look for three things: is it useful (solves the job), usable (easy to use), and does it delight (small moments that feel great)?
Product sense is the habit of noticing why things work or don't, and what you would change.

questions.prompt: Match each product to what makes it great.

pairs.right: Pay anyone in seconds for free
Simple messaging that works on any phone

questions.explain: Each one does one important job much better than the old way.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of 'delight'?
options: Swiggy showing the rider's live location and a fun message while you wait
questions.explain: Live tracking calms worry, and small touches make waiting feel better. That's delight on top of usefulness.

questions.prompt: A product with lots of features is always better.
questions.explain: More features can make it harder to use. WhatsApp won by staying simple.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 things that make a product good.
questions.explain: Useful, usable, delightful. Features and ads don't make a product good on their own.

questions.prompt: Which is not a sign of good product sense?
lines: Asking who the user is first
Copying every feature a rival adds
Cutting steps that don't help the user
questions.explain: Copying everything leads to a messy product. Good PMs choose what fits their users.

questions.prompt: Why did Instagram beat many photo apps early on?
options: It had the most editing tools
Fast, simple filters and sharing that made phone photos look good
questions.explain: One job done beautifully: take a photo, make it look nice, share it. Fast and simple.

questions.prompt: Put these steps to judge any product in order.
steps: What job does it do for them?
How well does it do that job?
questions.explain: Start with the user and job, then judge, then improve. This works in any interview.

lessons.title: Favourite product questions
teach: Interviewers often ask: 'What is your favourite product and why?' They want to see how you think, not which app you pick.
A strong answer names the user, the problem, why this product solves it well, one thing you would improve, and how you'd measure it.
Avoid only praising design. Talk about the user's problem and the business too.

questions.prompt: Put a strong 'favourite product' answer in order.
steps: Name the product and its main user
Explain why it solves it so well
questions.explain: User, problem, why it wins, what's next, and how to measure. Clear and complete.

questions.prompt: Which line is the weakest part of an answer?
options: It helps commuters know when the bus arrives
It cut my wait time and stress every day
I'd add alerts when the bus is 5 minutes away
questions.explain: Colour is a personal taste. It doesn't show product thinking about users or value.

questions.prompt: It's good to mention how the product makes money in your answer.
questions.explain: It shows you understand the business, not just the screens.

questions.prompt: Which improvement idea is weakest for Spotify?
lines: Better offline downloads for people with slow internet
Share a song to WhatsApp status with lyrics
questions.explain: A bigger logo doesn't solve any user problem.

questions.prompt: Match each product to a sensible success metric for an improvement.
questions.explain: Each metric shows whether the improvement actually helped the user.

questions.prompt: The interviewer asks 'who else uses it?'. What are they checking?
options: Whether you think beyond yourself to other user groups
questions.explain: You are not the only user. Good PMs think about other segments with different needs.

questions.prompt: You should pick an obscure app to impress the interviewer.
questions.explain: Pick one you know deeply. Depth beats novelty.

lessons.title: Design a product
teach: Design questions sound like: 'Design an app for elderly people to book doctors.' Don't jump to features.
Use a simple flow: clarify the goal, pick a user group, list their pains, pick one, brainstorm solutions, choose one, and measure it.
Picking one user and one pain is what makes your answer sharp.

questions.prompt: Put the design steps in order.
steps: Choose one pain and brainstorm ideas
Pick an idea and define how to measure it
questions.explain: Goal, user, pains, ideas, decision and metric. A calm structure stops you from rambling.

questions.prompt: For 'design a doctor booking app for elderly people', which pain is most specific?
options: Small text and many steps make booking hard alone
questions.explain: It is a real, specific barrier you can design for: bigger text, fewer steps, help from family.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 good ideas for that pain.
options: Book by voice or a call back
Let a family member book for them
questions.explain: Each idea removes a barrier. A feed or ads add clutter.

questions.prompt: In a design question, it's fine to ask a clarifying question first.
questions.explain: Asking about the goal or market shows you think before building.

questions.prompt: Which step is a mistake in a design answer?
lines: Asks what success means for the company
Picks elderly people in cities as the focus
Suggests measuring bookings completed without help
questions.explain: Listing many features without choosing shows no judgement. Prioritise.

questions.prompt: Match each design step to its question.

pairs.right: How will we know it worked?

questions.explain: Each step answers one clear question.

questions.prompt: What is a good success metric for the elderly booking app?
options: Share of bookings finished without calling for help
Number of colours in the app
questions.explain: It shows the app is truly easy for the chosen user.

lessons.title: Improve an existing product
teach: 'How would you improve Instagram?' is the twin of the design question. Start from who uses it and what bothers them.
Pick one user segment, find their top pain, suggest 2 or 3 ideas, choose one and say why.
Always check: does the idea help users and the business, and how hard is it to build?

questions.prompt: First step to answer 'Improve Uber'?
options: Choose a user group, like riders at airports or new drivers
questions.explain: Focus helps. Airport riders and new drivers have very different pains.

questions.prompt: Match the Uber user group to its pain.
questions.explain: Each group has its own top problem, so ideas differ.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 checks before choosing an idea.
options: How much it helps the user
How hard it is to build
Whether the CEO will like it
questions.explain: User value, business value and effort. That's how PMs prioritise.

questions.prompt: Which idea doesn't match the chosen pain 'finding the pickup point at airports'?
lines: Photos of the exact pickup spot
Live AR arrows to the pickup zone
Share live location between rider and driver
questions.explain: Loyalty points don't help someone lost at an airport.

questions.prompt: You should name a metric for your chosen improvement.
questions.explain: For pickup help, track time from driver arrival to rider pickup, or 'can't find you' calls.

questions.prompt: Order this improve answer.
steps: State the goal for the improvement
Choose one with reasons and a metric
questions.explain: Same shape as a design answer, but grounded in the existing product.

questions.prompt: Which reason for choosing an idea is strongest?
options: It solves the biggest pain for a large group and is quick to build
questions.explain: Big impact, many users, low effort. Clear trade-off thinking.
